sentences.text: Bagualia is an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur, a group of large herbivorous sauropods that evolved later than their earlier relatives. This classification places it within the parent group Eusauropoda, distinguishing it from more primitive forms.

The genus name Bagualia means "wild horse" in Spanish, referring to the discovery location Bagual Canyon. The species name alba means "dawn" in Spanish, highlighting the dinosaur's early position in the sauropod lineage.

The fossil record includes numerous bones, such as vertebrae, limb bones, and skull fragments from three individuals. In total, the remains consist of more than 200 bones, including axial elements, cervical vertebrae, appendicular bones, and cranial parts.

The skull of Bagualia is relatively complete and possesses a unique beak-like process at the front of the upper jaw that may have supported a large keratinous structure. The upper jaw contains 13 tooth sockets with some teeth preserved in various stages of eruption.

Bagualia is classified as an eusauropod based on features like its procumbent tooth arrangement. It had broad-crowned teeth suited for tougher vegetation, unlike the thinner-crowned teeth of Patagosaurus. These teeth had an enamel layer approximately 7 times thicker than other extinct herbivores, aiding in cutting conifer leaves.

Bagualia had a humerus and femur with increased eccentricity to resist bending forces in its large body. Features in the ulna and metacarpals indicate that Bagualia was an obligate quadruped. It possessed a laterally projecting cnemial crest on the tibia and a wedge-shaped astragalus for refined locomotion.
Bagualia is the oldest known definitive eusauropod dinosaur.

The type species Bagualia alba was formally described in 2020 by Pol et al. The genus Bagualia was named by Pol and colleagues in 2020.

Fossils of Bagualia were discovered in Bagual Canyon, about 4.3 km from Cerro Cóndor in Chubut, Argentina. The fossils were excavated by the Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio during fieldwork in 2007 and 2009.

Bagualia lived during the Early Jurassic, specifically the middle Toarcian stage. Bagualia fossils come from the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina, dated to 179 million years ago. Bagualia lived during the Toarcian stage, between 182.9 and 180.4 million years ago.

The holotype of Bagualia originates from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation. The depositional settings of Bagualia's habitat included tuffaceous materials, suggesting volcanic activity.
